extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, parties to PTAB AIA trials (petitioners and patent owners), and counsel appearing before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board
extracted.subtask_short: PTAB trial practice for AIA proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Practice guide setting out the procedures, substantive thresholds, evidence, discovery, confidentiality, and courtroom conduct for AIA trial proceedings (inter partes review, post-grant review, covered business method review, and derivation) before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition content and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings begin with the filing of a petition that identifies all of the claims challenged and the grounds and supporting evidence on a claim-by-claim basis; the petition must be filed consistent with any statute-required time periods and be accompanied by the evidence the petitioner seeks to rely upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For IPR, PGR, and CBM the patent owner may file a preliminary response within three months of notification of a filing date; petitions should include claim-by-claim grounds and supporting evidence. (References: 35 U.S.C. 135(a), 311(c), § 42.3.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for instituting a trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may institute a trial where the petitioner establishes that the standards for instituting the requested trial are met, taking into account any preliminary response; conversely, the Board may not institute where the petition (considering the preliminary response) fails to meet the requisite standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory references include 35 U.S.C. 314 (IPR) and 324 (PGR/CBM). Institution is discretionary and fact-specific; the Board evaluates the petition plus any preliminary response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing of issues at institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon institution, the Board will narrow the issues for final decision by authorizing trial only on challenged claims and specific grounds for which threshold standards are met; any claim or issue not included in the authorization will not be part of the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will identify on a claim-by-claim basis the grounds authorized for trial; dissatisfied parties may seek rehearing for overlooked or misapprehended points (see § 42.71).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling Order and one-year completion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board enters a Scheduling Order concurrent with the decision to institute a trial; the Scheduling Order sets due dates and ensures the trial is completed within one year of institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Scheduling Order accounts for complexity but maintains the one-year statutory target. Example sequencing consistent with §§ 42.120 and 42.220 was provided (patent owner response/motion to amend deadlines, petitioner replies, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequenced discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery proceeds in a sequenced fashion after institution (generally patent owner discovery first, then petitioner discovery), allowing meaningful discovery before motions and oppositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequencing focuses discovery on what parties reasonably need to respond to the grounds raised; the Scheduling Order sets times for each party's discovery windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of filings, motions, and oral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial conference call is held about one month from institution to discuss intended motions and adjust the Scheduling Order; patent owner may file a response and/or a motion to amend; petitioner may reply and oppose amendments; parties may file motions to exclude and thereafter have an opportunity for oral argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide outlines a representative timeline: patent owner response/motion to amend, petitioner reply/opposition, patent owner reply in support of amendments, motions to exclude, then oral hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: General objectives of the rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules are to be construed to ensure the just, speedy, and inexpensive resolution of a proceeding and may be modified to accomplish these goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See § 42.1(b) and § 42.5(a),(b). The Board balances timeliness, fairness, and efficiency in applying or modifying procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board jurisdiction over involved patents/applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has exclusive jurisdiction within the Office over every application and patent that is involved in a derivation, IPR, PGR, or CBM proceeding; ex parte and inter partes reexamination proceedings are not 'involved' and are treated separately except as ordered by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdictional rules are based on 35 U.S.C. 6(b) and related statutes; coordination with other Office matters is possible by Board order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on ex parte communications
rubrics_metrics.description: All substantive communications with the Board regarding a proceeding must include all parties to the proceeding, except as otherwise authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include ministerial communications with support staff, conference calls/hearings where opposing counsel declines to participate, informing the Board of related Board proceedings, and referencing a pending case to support a general proposition. See § 42.5(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and management of conference calls
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board encourages conference calls to raise and resolve issues quickly; parties should be prepared to explain the need and materials required for the call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party refuses to participate, the Board may permit a call without them and impose safeguards (e.g., recording the call and entering it into the record). Procedural issues are expected to be handled within days via conference call or shortly thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel designation and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: A party represented by counsel must designate both a lead and a back-up counsel; a power of attorney must be filed with counsel designation unless counsel is already of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead counsel is expected to participate in hearings and sign filings; back-up counsel should be able to conduct business if lead counsel is unavailable. See § 42.10(a)-(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro hac vice and conduct of counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may recognize counsel pro hac vice for good cause, provided lead counsel is a registered practitioner; the Board may impose conditions and revoke pro hac vice for incompetence, violations of professional conduct rules, or incivility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting pro hac vice is discretionary, considering the technical complexity of proceedings and the specifics of the case (see § 42.10(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic filing as default
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic filing is the default manner for submissions to the Board; paper filings are allowed only with a motion explaining the need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single uploaded file may exceed 250 megabytes; parties encountering electronic filing problems during normal business hours may contact the Board for a one-day extension; the Board will publish electronic submission info on its website. See § 42.6(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory notices (real parties-in-interest, related matters, counsel, service info)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must provide mandatory notices identifying real parties-in-interest and privies, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information; changes must be filed within 21 days of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice requirements assist the Board in identifying potential conflicts and applying estoppel; see § 42.8 and § 42.8(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real party-in-interest and privy disclosure and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must identify real parties-in-interest and privies to assist the Board in identifying conflicts and applying statutory estoppel; determination is fact-dependent and assessed case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide explains that common-law principles and cases (e.g., Taylor v. Sturgell) guide the analysis; funding/control of a petition is a typical example where a funder that directs/controls the petition is a real party-in-interest. There is no bright-line test; assessments consider control, relationships to the petition, and other equitable factors. CBM proceedings require that the petitioner or its RPI/privy has been sued for infringement or charged with infringement under that patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related matters disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must identify any judicial or administrative matter that would affect or be affected by the decision in the proceeding, including federal court actions, applications/patents claiming priority, and ex parte or inter partes reexaminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This disclosure helps the Board coordinate and consider estoppel or overlapping issues across forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service information and correspondence responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are required to identify service information to allow efficient communication; the applicant or patent owner remains responsible for maintaining a proper correspondence address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under § 42.6(e) parties may agree that electronic filing with the Board constitutes electronic service; Ray v. Lehman cited on correspondence responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability of the record and sealing procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of a proceeding shall be made available to the public except as otherwise ordered; documents are public unless a party files and the Board grants a motion to seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to seal can be filed concurrent with the document; documents are provisionally sealed pending the Board's decision. See § 42.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and protection of confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential information is identified consistent with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(c)(1)(G) (trade secret or other confidential research, development, or commercial information); protective orders may be issued for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines and a default Standing Protective Order are provided in Appendix B; protective orders protect trade secrets and other sensitive information while balancing public file history interests. See § 42.54.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling confidential information filed with petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner filing confidential information with a petition may file a motion to seal with a proposed protective order concurrent with the filing and is not required to serve the confidential information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner access prior to institution is available by agreeing to the default protective order, agreeing to petitioner’s proposed order, filing a joint protective order, or upon Board entry of a protective order. See § 42.55.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expungement and timing for public disclosure of confidential info
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential information under protective order ordinarily becomes public 45 days after denial of a petition to institute or 45 days after final judgment in a trial; parties may file a motion to expunge information before it becomes public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule balances confidentiality with public notice/file history; parties are encouraged to redact sensitive portions rather than seal entire documents. See § 42.56.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation-specific confidentiality (conception dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivation proceedings, parties submitting dates of conception to establish inventorship may file such information under seal and request that an opponent not be given access to conception dates until the opponent has provided their conception dates to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision helps protect sensitive inventorship evidence while allowing a fair comparison once both sides' dates are submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposal and destruction of confidential information after final termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Within one month after final termination of a proceeding (including appeals) or within one month after the time for appeal has expired, each party shall assemble all copies of confidential information received, destroy it, and provide a certification of destruction to the producing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must ensure confidential materials (including those provided to representatives and experts) are collected and destroyed and certify destruction to the producing party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of routine discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine discovery includes production of any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony, cross-examination of the other side’s declarants, and relevant information inconsistent with a position advanced during the proceeding; Board authorization is not required for routine discovery though the Board sets the timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine discovery is designed to place parties on a level playing field and streamline proceedings; times are set in the Scheduling Order. See § 42.51(b)(1) and related text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of inconsistent statements/evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must disclose non-privileged work or evidence that is inconsistent with contentions relied upon in affidavits or testimony (e.g., laboratory work inconsistent with an expert’s affidavit or evidence inconsistent with ‘unexpected results’ arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: petitioner relying on an expert affidavit asserting non-practicability must produce non-privileged work inconsistent with that contention; patent owner relying on unexpected results must produce inconsistent non-privileged evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness production expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden and expense of producing a witness for redirect or cross-examination normally falls on the party presenting the witness; this applies to employed witnesses, experts, and non-party witnesses and to transcripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If testimony is presented by affidavit or transcript, the presenting party should make the witness available and bear associated fees and travel expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document translation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All proceedings before the Board will be conducted in English; translations must be provided for documents produced in discovery and for all documents relied on or otherwise used during the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations are required to ensure a complete and understandable record in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to depose declarants supporting amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent owner relies upon new declaration evidence in support of claim amendments, the petitioner will be authorized to depose those declarants and submit observations on the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequenced discovery anticipates depositions tied to filings; Board will authorize depositions consistent with Scheduling Order and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to exclude evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once discovery time has ended, parties may file motions to exclude evidence believed to be inadmissible; admissibility is generally governed by the Federal Rules of Evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions to exclude are typically filed after discovery and before oral hearing; the Board follows Federal Rules of Evidence principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination by settlement or lack of petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner and patent owner may terminate the proceeding with respect to the petitioner by filing a written agreement with the Board unless the Board has decided the merits; if no petitioner remains, the Board may terminate review or proceed to a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See statutory references 35 U.S.C. 317 and 327; the Board's discretion depends on whether merits have been decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model ESI (e-discovery) streamlining and cost-shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: ESI production is streamlined to promote just, speedy, and inexpensive resolution; costs will be shifted for disproportionate ESI production requests and nonresponsive or dilatory tactics will be considered in cost-shifting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Model Order supplements discovery rules, may be modified for good cause, and considers parties' meaningful compliance when allocating costs. See Appendix C.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI production metadata and email limits
rubrics_metrics.description: General ESI production shall not include metadata (with limited exceptions such as date/time and distribution list); email is excluded from general ESI production and requires specific Board-authorized requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fields showing date/time and distribution list should generally be included if they exist. Email production requires prior authorization and specific, narrowly tailored requests. See Appendix C paragraphs 5-6.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI email production mechanics (custodians and search terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When email production is authorized, requests must be issue-specific, phased after initial productions, identify custodian(s), search terms, and time frame, and be narrowly tailored; default limits are five custodians per producing party and five search terms per custodian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may agree to modify limits; the Board may authorize additional custodians/search terms on showing of need. Conjunctive combinations count as one search term; disjunctive combinations count separately unless variants. Overbroad terms (e.g., company/product names) are inappropriate without narrowing. See Appendix C paragraphs 6-11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege protection and inadvertent ESI production
rubrics_metrics.description: The receiving party shall not use ESI that the producing party asserts is attorney-client privileged or work product protected to challenge privilege or protection; inadvertent production of privileged ESI is not a waiver if reasonable steps to prevent disclosure were taken and prompt reasonable steps to rectify were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Model Order follows Federal Rule of Evidence 502 principles and treats mass productions consistently with Rule 502(d) protections. See Appendix C paragraphs 12-13.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony format and examination conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncompelled direct testimony is almost always presented by affidavit or declaration (§ 42.53(a)); all other testimony (cross-examination, redirect, compelled direct testimony) occurs by oral examination; cross-examination should be a question-and-answer conversation with no coaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary or speaking objections and coaching are prohibited; examination follows Federal Rules of Civil Procedure practices supplemented by district court practices; counsel must not act as intermediary interpreting questions during witness testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection rules and examination recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections must be noted on the record but testimony proceeds subject to the objection; objections must be concise, non-argumentative, and non-suggestive; testimony must be recorded by audio, audiovisual, or stenographic means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper objections: e.g., 'Objection, form,' 'Objection, hearsay.' Improper: argumentative or suggestive statements. An objection explanation must be provided if requested or it is waived. See Testimony Guidelines and Appendix D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on counsel communications during cross-examination and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once cross-examination has commenced, counsel offering the witness shall not consult with the witness about the substance of testimony already given or anticipated except to assert privilege or comply with Board order; the Board may impose sanctions (including fees) for impeding or frustrating fair examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel shall not initiate private conferences with witnesses or call breaks while a question is pending except to determine whether to assert a privilege; parties may move to terminate/limit testimony for bad-faith conduct but must promptly conference the Board. See Appendix D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing Protective Order required markings and access categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential information must be clearly marked 'PROTECTIVE ORDER MATERIAL'; access is limited to enumerated categories: parties, party representatives, retained experts (with certification they are not competitors), in-house counsel, other employees with agreement or Board order, Office employees, and reasonable support personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standing Protective Order is automatically entered upon filing a petition or institution of a derivation; Appendix B provides detailed access, acknowledgement form, and duties to maintain confidentiality (secure storage, limited copying, informing support staff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for filing confidential and redacted versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where confidentiality is alleged for only part of a submission, the submitting party should file confidential and non-confidential versions plus a Motion to Seal setting out reasons; non-confidential version must indicate redacted locations and the confidential version is filed under seal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board treats the confidential submission as provisionally sealed pending motion outcome; redaction is encouraged over sealing entire documents. See Standing Protective Order §4 and §42.14 guidance.
